title: Shared clinical equipment and surface barriers
audience: Cleaning staff who work on equipment and surfaces passed between several patients.
learningOutcomes: Pinpoint the handled areas on shared clinical equipment.
State the cleaning rule for shared equipment between patients.
Describe when a surface barrier is used and how it is replaced.

instruction.heading: Why shared equipment matters
instruction.body: Shared clinical equipment only meets intact skin, so it is unlikely to infect anyone directly. It can still act as a carrier, moving organisms from one patient to the next through the parts that hands and skin touch during care. The guideline's examples are the knobs and handles on dialysis units, x-ray units, instrument carts and dental chairs.

instruction.heading: The cleaning rule
instruction.body: Between patients, wipe the handled parts of shared equipment with a detergent mix. Any departure needs a documented risk assessment to back it. Frequencies for particular shared items sit in the B5.1 table, the same reference relied on in “High-touch items: minimum intervals for patient rooms” and “Beds, equipment, curtains and mattresses: minimum frequencies”.

instruction.heading: Surface barriers
instruction.body: A moisture-impermeable covering, such as cling film, a plastic bag, a sheet, or tubing, forms a barrier between contamination and equipment. Fit it so that all parts requiring protection are enclosed, then strip it off and disinfect what lies underneath between patients. Where no covering can be applied, cleaning the surface still applies.

instruction.heading: When a barrier is required
instruction.body: Put a barrier on equipment that gloved hands handle repeatedly during treatment, on items prone to splatter from bodily fluids, and on surfaces that are awkward to clean. Leaving any of these uncovered needs a documented risk analysis. The guideline lists air-water syringes, bed boards and keyboards as illustrations.

procedure: Locate the shared equipment in the room and mark its touched parts, such as handles, knobs and keypads.
Strip the barrier off the item and dispose of it according to the waste rules for that area.
Wipe the touched parts with a detergent mix after each patient.
Fit a new barrier so it fully covers the surface beneath and does not block a control.
Check the barrier is secure and that no fluid has passed through it.
Log the item, its timing, and the barrier replacement.

workedExamples.situation: A dental chair and its control arm have just been used on a patient. The next patient is due in ten minutes.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should happen before the next patient?
workedExamples.reasoning: Strip and bin the barrier on the arm, wipe the touched parts with a detergent mix, and fit a new barrier that covers the surface beneath. Log the change.

equipmentAndPpe: Barrier stock of the approved type
Waste bag for used barrier material

commonErrors.error: Leaving a barrier in place for two patients to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Replace barriers between patients, as the guideline requires.

commonErrors.error: Treating a barrier as a substitute for cleaning.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean the surface even where a barrier was used; if no barrier could be fitted, cleaning still applies.

commonErrors.error: Fitting a barrier that blocks a control or a display.
commonErrors.prevention: Position the barrier to protect the surface without hiding the function of the equipment.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Never reuse a barrier that has been on a patient. Dispose of it under the area's waste rules.
Powered equipment is cleaned only as the maker directs. Keep liquid away from connections and vents.

qualityStandard: Touched parts of shared equipment are wiped between each patient.
Barriers are replaced between patients and sit over the surface beneath.
Any departure from the rule is tied to a risk assessment on file.
documentationEvidence: Shared equipment clean log with item, time and patient changeover
Barrier change record, with any exception and its risk assessment reference
summary: Shared equipment can carry infection between patients through the parts people touch.
Wipe touched parts with a detergent mix between patients; exceptions need a risk assessment.
Barriers are replaced between patients and do not replace cleaning.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which requirement applies to wiping the touched sections of shared clinical kit?
options: Clean them once, as the week closes and again at the start of each shift and before lunch
Wipe them with a detergent mix between patients, unless a documented risk assessment justifies an exception.
Clean only the parts a patient can see and leave the rest until the end of the month each time
Clean them only if the patient complains and only on the day the complaint is made to the manager

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is an example of shared equipment the guideline names?
options: A bed sheet folded and stored on a shelf.
A dental chair, an x-ray unit or a dialysis unit.
A paper towel dispenser in a staff room.
A cleaning cupboard, a mop bucket and a spare linen trolley

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen to a surface barrier between patients?
options: It is left in place and reused.
It is replaced, and the surface beneath is cleaned.
It is washed in a domestic washing machine.
It is allowed to dry, then moved to the next patient.

sourceReferences: Australian Guidelines for Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, B1.4.2 (shared clinical equipment; surface barriers; Recommendations 12 and 13); rights: not held by user; reworded (no copying)
Source priority: the NHMRC guideline is an official Australian source. Where it conflicts with informal or in-house cleaning advice, the guideline governs the points this lesson relies on.

Australian Guidelines for Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare, edition note: the 2019 edition is the current edition (NHMRC, https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-05/australian-guidelines-for-the-prevention-and-control-of-infection-in-healthcare.pdf; CONFIRMED in the figures register, checked 2026-11-02); the uploaded copy read on 2026-11-02 is the 2010 edition, so points taken from it are UNCONFIRMED against the 2019 text. The existing aged-care and medical-equipment lessons cite the 2019 edition.
